title: Start Freelancing: Fiverr, Upwork & Your First Client
tagline: Choose a skill people pay for, build a profile clients trust, win your first project and grow a safe, steady freelance business from Pakistan.

description:
Freelancing lets you sell your skills to clients in your city and around the world, from your own laptop. But many beginners make accounts, wait, and give up. This course shows you, step by step, how to start properly and grow safely.

**Basic stages (free):**

- **The Starting Line:** what freelancing really is and how to choose one skill people already pay for.
- **The Market Square:** how marketplaces work, the difference between Fiverr-style gigs and Upwork-style proposals in general terms, and why platform rules matter.
- **The Shop Window:** a strong profile, honest samples and your first gig or proposal.

**Advanced stages (Premium):**

- **The Pitch Room:** winning proposals, pricing with a method, handling price pressure and earning honest reviews.
- **The Workshop:** scope, revisions, written agreements, time management and difficult clients.
- **The Growth Road:** getting paid from abroad in general terms, records and taxes, avoiding scams and building repeat clients and a personal brand.

We teach skills, not fast-changing details: platform fees, rules and payment methods change, so the course shows you how to check the current terms yourself. Follow Ayesha, Bilal, Nasreen and their mentor Kamran as they find, serve and keep their first clients.

sessions.title: What Freelancing Is and Choosing a Skill People Will Pay For
sessions.summary: Understand what freelancing really means, how it differs from a job, and how to pick one skill that clients already pay for and you can deliver well, so you start with a clear, honest offer.
objectives: Explain what freelancing is and how it differs from a salaried job
Tell the difference between a hobby, a skill and a sellable service
Choose one starting skill using demand, your ability and your available time
Describe your first service in one clear, client-focused sentence

cards.title: Rs 0 and a laptop
cards.setting: A small rooftop room in Lahore, late evening. Ayesha's final-year exams are over.

lines.text: Welcome to the First Client Quest. Ayesha has a laptop, good internet on most days and a big wish: to earn from home.
Everyone says 'start freelancing'. But start what? I can design a bit, write a bit, edit videos a bit. Where do I even begin?
(video call from Karachi) Same here! I made accounts on three sites last night. Nobody has messaged me yet.
Accounts are not a business. A business starts with one clear answer: what problem will you solve, and for whom?
So I should not try to sell everything I can do?
Exactly. Pick one skill that people already pay for, that you can deliver well, and that fits your time. That is your first mission.

scenes.heading: You are the business
scenes.narration: A freelancer sells a service to clients, project by project, instead of working for one employer on a salary. You decide what to offer, whom to work with and when to work.

scenes.heading: Clients buy results
scenes.narration: Clients do not pay for your effort or your degree. They pay for a result: a logo that looks professional, a website that works, a translated document that reads naturally.

scenes.heading: Clients can be anywhere
scenes.narration: Online marketplaces and social media let a designer in Lahore work for a café in Karachi or a shop in another country. Distance matters less than trust and quality.

scenes.heading: Freedom comes with duties
scenes.narration: There is no fixed salary, no paid leave and no manager to plan your day. You find clients, manage time, keep records and handle payment yourself.

scenes.heading: Start small, grow steadily
scenes.narration: Most freelancers begin with small projects, earn their first reviews and grow from there. Steady progress beats overnight success stories.

cards.question: Ayesha says, 'Clients will hire me because I have a design degree.' What does Kamran most likely tell her?
options: Clients mostly pay for a clear result that solves their problem
A degree is the only thing clients look at before hiring
Clients prefer people who list as many skills as possible
cards.explanation: A degree can help, but clients choose freelancers who show they can deliver the result they need, for example through samples and a clear offer.

cards.title: Hobby, skill or sellable service?
cards.body:
A **hobby** is something you enjoy. A **skill** is something you can do well. A **sellable service** is a skill packaged to solve a specific problem that people already spend money on.

For example, 'I like drawing' is a hobby. 'I can design in a design tool' is a skill. 'I design clean social media posts for small food businesses' is a service a client can understand and buy.

A good starting service has three things:

- **Demand:** people already search for it and pay for it.
- **Ability:** you can deliver it to a good standard today, not 'one day'.
- **Fit:** it suits your time, tools and internet.

Bilal has built three working websites for friends' shops

cards.title: Ten skills or one?
cards.situation: Bilal can build websites, edit videos, write blog posts, do data entry and fix laptops. He wants to put all of them on his profile so that 'more people find him'. He has about three hours each evening after his job search. What should he do?

choices.text: Choose one main service, such as simple websites for small shops, and build his profile and samples around it.
choices.outcome: Best choice. A focused offer is easier for clients to understand and trust. He can add related services later once he has reviews.

choices.text: List all his skills so that he appears in more searches.
choices.outcome: This feels safe, but clients often skip profiles that look unfocused. 'Jack of all trades' is hard to trust for a specific job.

choices.text: Choose two closely related services, such as websites and website updates.
choices.outcome: Acceptable. Related services can support each other, but he should still lead with one clear main offer.

choices.text: Wait until he has mastered every skill before starting.
choices.outcome: Waiting for perfect slows him down. He already has one skill that is ready to sell; he can start there.

cards.title: How Ayesha chose her first service
cards.body:
Ayesha listed everything she could do: posters, logos, a bit of writing and some video editing. Then she asked three questions for each.

- **Do people pay for it?** She looked at what small businesses near her asked for in local groups and on marketplaces. Social media posts and simple logos came up again and again.
- **Can I deliver it well today?** She had a folder of strong posters but only rough video edits.
- **Does it fit my time?** Posts are short projects she can finish in an evening.

Her first service became: **'Eye-catching social media posts for small food and clothing businesses.'** Video editing went on her 'practise first' list.

cards.question: Which description is the strongest first service for a beginner?
options: Graphic design, writing, editing, data entry and more
Clean menu and price-list design for local cafés and restaurants
Creative person who loves art and new challenges
Anything design-related at the lowest price online
cards.explanation: It names a specific result and a specific type of client. The others are vague, describe a personality or compete only on price.

cards.title: Be honest about time
cards.body: Freelancing beside studies or a job is common. Decide how many hours a week you can really give, and choose a service that fits. A client who is promised 'tomorrow' and receives it next week will not come back. Promise less, deliver on time, and you build trust from the very first project.

cards.title: Take-aways from the Starting Line
items: A freelancer runs a small business: finding clients, doing the work, managing time and handling payment.
Clients pay for results that solve their problems, not for effort or titles.
A sellable service has demand, your proven ability and a good fit with your time.
Start with one focused service and a clear type of client; add more later.
Describe your service in one sentence that names the result and the client.

cards.prompt: Write down three skills you have. For each, ask: do people pay for it, can I deliver it well today, and does it fit my time? Which one becomes your first service, and how would you describe it in one sentence?

quiz.question: What best describes a freelancer?
options: Someone who works for one company on a monthly salary
Someone who only works on hobbies in their free time
Someone who sells services to clients project by project
Someone who resells products bought from wholesale markets
quiz.explanation: A freelancer runs their own small service business and works for different clients on separate projects.

quiz.question: Which is a duty a freelancer must usually handle personally?
options: Finding clients and planning their own working time
Waiting for a manager to assign daily tasks
Receiving paid leave arranged by an employer
Following the office hours set out in a company's staff handbook
quiz.explanation: Freelancers do not have an employer finding work or planning their day, so these jobs fall to them.

quiz.question: Ayesha enjoys drawing, can use design software well and offers 'menu design for cafés'. Which of these is the sellable service?
options: Enjoying drawing
Using design software well
Her design degree certificate
Menu design for cafés
quiz.explanation: A sellable service packages a skill to solve a specific problem for a specific client. Enjoyment is a hobby and software use is a skill.

quiz.question: Which three checks help you choose a starting service?
options: Lowest price, most skills and fastest delivery
Demand, your ability today and fit with your time
What friends do, what is trending and what pays most
Your degree, your age and your city
quiz.explanation: A good first service is something clients already pay for, that you can deliver well now, and that suits your hours, tools and internet.

quiz.question: On the skill and demand grid, where should a beginner start?
options: High skill level but very little client demand
High client demand and high skill level
High client demand but very little skill yet
Low client demand and low skill level
quiz.explanation: Start where people want the work and you can already deliver it well. Grow the other skills over time.

quiz.question: Why do many clients skip profiles that list ten unrelated skills?
options: Marketplaces ban profiles with more than one skill
Clients only hire people with a single university degree
Unrelated skills always make prices look too high
The offer looks unfocused and is harder to trust
quiz.explanation: Clients hire for a specific problem. A focused profile makes it easy to see that you are the right person for it.

quiz.question: Bilal has three free hours each evening. A client asks for a large website 'by tomorrow'. What is the most professional response?
options: Explain a realistic delivery date that fits his available hours
Accept and hope he can finish it in time somehow
Ignore the message because the deadline is unfair
Accept and ask a friend to secretly do half of it
quiz.explanation: Honest, realistic promises build trust. Overpromising and missing the deadline damages his reputation from the start.

quiz.question: Which of these is a 'niche'?
options: A list of every tool you know how to use
The total price of a finished project
Product photos for home-based clothing brands
The written review a client leaves after the final delivery
quiz.explanation: A niche is a focused area or type of client you choose to serve so that you stand out from general offers.

quiz.question: A beginner has watched video-editing tutorials but never edited a full video. Where does this skill belong for now?
options: At the very top of the profile, presented as the main service on offer
Nowhere, because video editing has no demand
In a proposal promising expert-level editing
On a 'practise first' list until there are real samples
quiz.explanation: Practise and create sample work first. Selling a skill you cannot yet deliver well risks unhappy clients and poor reviews.

quiz.question: What do clients mainly pay a freelancer for?
options: The number of hours the freelancer spent learning
A result that solves their problem
The freelancer's personal story and hobbies
The number of skills listed on the profile
quiz.explanation: Clients care about the outcome: a working website, a clear logo, a well-written page.

sessions.title: How Freelance Marketplaces Work: Gigs, Proposals and Trust
sessions.summary: See how online marketplaces connect clients and freelancers, the difference between selling a ready-made gig and sending a proposal for a posted job, how trust and payment protection work in general, and why you should always read the current platform rules.
objectives: Explain the role of a marketplace between clients and freelancers
Compare the gig model (as on Fiverr) with the proposal model (as on Upwork) in general terms
Describe the usual life of an order or contract from first message to review
Recognise common platform rules, such as keeping communication and payment on the platform
Know to check the current terms, because fees and rules change

cards.title: Two sites, two ways of working
cards.setting: Bilal's room in Karachi, Saturday morning. Ayesha and Kamran join on a video call.

lines.text: On one site I made a 'gig' and I wait. On the other I have to write proposals to jobs. Why are they so different?
And which one is better? I only want to learn one.
Think of a market. On Fiverr you mostly set up a stall with a fixed menu, and buyers walk past and order.
On Upwork, mostly, clients put up a notice saying 'I need this', and freelancers apply with a proposal.
So one is like a shop and the other is like applying for small jobs!
That is a good start. Both can work. Learn how each one builds trust, follow its rules, and you will not waste months.

scenes.heading: A meeting place
scenes.narration: A freelance marketplace is a website where clients look for services and freelancers offer them. It brings both sides together in one place.

scenes.heading: Search and matching
scenes.narration: Clients search, filter and browse. The site decides which profiles or offers to show first, using signals such as relevance, reviews and activity. Exactly how it decides is not public and can change.

scenes.heading: Payment handling
scenes.narration: In general, the client pays through the platform and the platform releases the money to the freelancer when the work is delivered or approved. This protects both sides when rules are followed.

scenes.heading: Reviews build trust
scenes.narration: After a project, clients usually leave a rating and a review. New clients read these to decide whom to trust, so every project shapes your future.

scenes.heading: Rules and fees
scenes.narration: Each platform has its own terms of service and charges fees in its own way. These change over time, so always read the current terms on the platform itself.

cards.title: How trust works on a marketplace
cards.body:
Clients cannot meet you, so they look for **signals of trust**:

- A **complete, honest profile** with a clear photo and description.
- **Work samples** that match the job they need.
- **Reviews** from earlier clients.
- **Quick, polite replies** to messages.
- **Delivering on time** without disputes.

When you are new you have no reviews, so the other signals matter even more. Platforms also use their own signals to decide what to show in search. They do not publish the exact formula and they change it, so focus on what you control: quality, honesty and good communication.

items.label: Agree the details

items.label: Order or contract starts
items.detail: The client pays or funds the work through the platform.

items.label: You deliver
items.detail: Share the work through the platform, on time.

items.label: Revisions and approval
items.detail: Make agreed changes; the client accepts the delivery.

items.label: Payment and review
items.detail: Funds are released in line with the platform's process, and both sides leave feedback.

cards.title: Usually fine or usually against the rules?
cards.prompt: Platform rules differ and change, but these patterns are common. Sort each action.

items.text: Asking a client questions about the project in the platform chat
Asking a new client to pay you directly to 'save on fees'
Writing your personal phone number in your gig description
Asking a friend to order your gig so you get a review
Sharing work samples that you created yourself
Delivering the files through the platform's delivery button
Opening a second account after the first was restricted

cards.title: 'Let's move to WhatsApp'
cards.situation: A new client messages Ayesha on a marketplace: 'I like your posts. Give me your WhatsApp and I will pay you directly by bank transfer. It is cheaper for both of us.' She has not worked with this client before.

choices.text: Thank the client and explain that she keeps communication and payment on the platform, as its rules require, then offer to start an order there.
choices.outcome: Best choice. It keeps her account in good standing and keeps the protection the platform gives both sides if something goes wrong.

choices.text: Send her WhatsApp number and agree, because it saves on fees.
choices.outcome: Risky. Many platforms forbid taking new clients off the platform, which can get the account restricted, and she loses payment protection if the client never pays.

choices.text: Ignore the message completely.
choices.outcome: She avoids the risk but may lose a genuine client. A polite reply that offers to work on the platform is better.

cards.title: Read the rules where they live
cards.body: Fees, payment timings, account levels and rules are different on each platform and they change. Do not rely on a video or a friend's advice from last year. Read the current terms of service and help pages on the platform itself before you start, and check again from time to time.

cards.question: A YouTube video says a platform's fee is a certain amount and payments arrive in a certain number of days. What should Ayesha do?
options: Plan her whole pricing around the video's numbers
Check the current terms on the platform's own pages
Assume all platforms charge exactly the same
cards.explanation: Fees and timings vary by platform and change over time. The platform's own current terms are the reliable source.

cards.front: 'Make an account and orders will come.'
cards.back: Myth. You need a clear offer, samples, a strong profile and often many proposals or gig improvements before the first order.

cards.front: 'You can only freelance on big marketplaces.'
cards.back: Myth. Many freelancers also find clients through referrals, LinkedIn, local business groups and their own websites.
Fact. New clients read reviews to decide whom to trust, so every project counts.
Myth. Terms, fees and processes differ, so read each one's current rules.

cards.title: Take-aways from the Market Square
items: A marketplace connects clients and freelancers, handles payment in general and shows reviews.
Gig model: you publish a ready-made offer and buyers order. Proposal model: clients post jobs and you apply.
Trust comes from an honest profile, matching samples, reviews, quick replies and on-time delivery.
Keep communication and payment on the platform where its rules require it; this also keeps you protected.
Fees and rules vary and change: always check the current terms on the platform itself.

cards.prompt: Which way of working suits you better right now: a ready-made gig or tailored proposals? Think about your service, your time and how comfortable you are writing to clients. What will you check in the platform's current terms before you start?

quiz.question: What is the main role of a freelance marketplace?
options: Connecting clients with freelancers and handling the deal
Employing freelancers on a fixed monthly salary
Teaching freelancers every skill they will need
Guaranteeing every freelancer a steady, reliable flow of new orders
quiz.explanation: Marketplaces bring both sides together, usually handle payment and show reviews. They do not employ you or guarantee work.

quiz.question: In the gig model, as on Fiverr, who usually makes the first move?
options: The client, by posting a detailed job notice for sellers to answer
The platform, by assigning work to sellers
The freelancer, by publishing a ready-made offer
A recruiter, who interviews each freelancer
quiz.explanation: In the gig model you set up an offer with packages in advance, and buyers find it and order.

quiz.question: In the proposal model, as on Upwork, what is the freelancer's main task?
options: Designing an attractive gig image and then waiting for buyers to order
Writing a tailored proposal for each suitable job
Uploading a CV and waiting to be employed
Sending the same message to every client
quiz.explanation: Clients post jobs and freelancers respond with proposals that show they understand that specific need.

quiz.question: Why does a platform usually handle payment between client and freelancer?
options: It allows the freelancer to skip delivering work
It lets the client avoid paying for finished work
It removes the need for any agreement on scope
It gives both sides a level of protection when rules are followed
quiz.explanation: In general the platform holds or processes payment and releases it under its process, which protects both sides. Exact protection depends on the platform's current terms.

quiz.question: A client asks you to share your WhatsApp and pay you outside the platform before any work. What is the main risk?
options: Your internet connection may become slower
The client may end up leaving you far too many good reviews
Breaking platform rules and losing payment protection
Your design files may become too large to send
quiz.explanation: Many platforms forbid moving new clients off-platform, and you would lose the platform's protection if the client did not pay.

quiz.question: Which is a strong trust signal for a new freelancer with no reviews yet?
options: Work samples that match the job the client needs
A very long list of unrelated skills
A profile with no photo and only a short, general bio about hobbies
A promise to work for free for a month
quiz.explanation: Without reviews, matching samples, a complete profile and quick, polite replies carry most of the trust.

quiz.question: Bilal reads in an old blog post how a platform ranks profiles in search. What is the sensible view?
options: The blog post is the official and permanent formula
Search ranking is purely random and nothing helps
Paying a stranger for reviews is the best strategy
Ranking methods are not fully public and change, so focus on quality
quiz.explanation: Platforms do not publish their exact formulas and change them. Honest quality, good communication and on-time delivery are what you control.

quiz.question: What is a 'milestone' on a fixed-price project?
options: A bonus paid when a client is very happy
A part of the project with its own delivery and payment
The platform's fee for every new proposal
A rating a client gives after five projects
quiz.explanation: Breaking a fixed-price project into milestones lets each part be delivered and paid for in turn.

quiz.question: Ayesha asks a cousin to order her gig and leave a five-star review. Why is this a bad idea?
options: Cousins cannot open accounts on any platform
Five-star reviews always lower a gig's ranking
Fake reviews are dishonest and usually break platform rules
Reviews are never shown to new clients
quiz.explanation: Fake orders and reviews mislead clients and are usually against the terms; accounts can be restricted for them.

quiz.question: Where should you check a platform's current fees and payment timings?
options: The platform's own current terms and help pages
A friend's message from a few years ago
Any video with the most views on the topic
The comments section under a popular social media post
quiz.explanation: Fees and rules change. The platform's own current pages are the reliable source.

sessions.title: Building a Strong Profile and Your First Gig or Proposal
sessions.summary: Turn your service into a profile that clients trust: a clear headline, a client-focused overview, honest samples and a first gig or proposal that answers the client's real question, 'Can you solve my problem?'
objectives: Write a clear headline and a client-focused profile overview
Create honest sample work when you have no clients yet
Set up a first gig with a clear title, packages, description and requirements
Write a short first proposal that is tailored to one job
Avoid dishonest shortcuts such as copied portfolios and fake claims

cards.title: A profile all about me
cards.setting: Ayesha's rooftop room, Lahore. She shares her screen with Kamran in Islamabad.

lines.text: Here is my profile: 'I am a passionate, hard-working and creative designer who loves colours.' Good, no?
Read it as a café owner who needs posts for Eid. What does it tell you about your problem?
Hmm. Nothing. It only talks about me.
(joining from Faisalabad) As a client, I want to know three things fast: can you do my kind of work, can I see it, and will you be on time.
Nasreen runs a pickle business and hires freelancers. Listen to her. Your profile is a shop window, and the client is the one walking past.

cards.title: What makes a client stop and read

scenes.heading: Clear in seconds
scenes.narration: A client scrolls through many profiles. Your photo, headline and first lines must show, in seconds, what you do and for whom.

scenes.heading: About their problem
scenes.narration: Talk about the client's result: 'posts that make your menu look delicious', not 'I am passionate'. Show you understand what they want.

scenes.heading: Proof you can do it
scenes.narration: Samples are stronger than adjectives. Two or three good pieces that match your service beat a long list of claims.

scenes.heading: Easy to say yes
scenes.narration: Explain what is included, what you need from the client and how long it takes. Fewer questions mean faster decisions.

cards.title: Building blocks of a strong profile
cards.caption: Complete each block honestly. Menus and field names can change between platform versions.

items.label: Clear photo
items.detail: A friendly, well-lit photo of you, so clients know a real person is behind the profile.

items.label: Headline
items.detail: One line naming your service and client, e.g. 'Social media posts for food businesses'.

items.label: Overview
items.detail: A short paragraph about the client's problem, your solution and how you work.

items.label: Portfolio
items.detail: Two to five honest samples that match your service.

items.label: Skills and details
items.detail: Relevant skills, languages and any real qualifications.

cards.title: Writing a client-focused overview
cards.body:
A simple structure works well:

1. **The client's need:** 'Running a small food business is busy. Your social media still needs to look fresh.'
2. **What you do:** 'I design clear, colourful posts and stories that show your dishes at their best.'
3. **How you work:** 'You send your menu and photos; I deliver ready-to-post designs with one round of changes included.'
4. **A simple invitation:** 'Message me with your next offer or event and I will suggest ideas.'

Use short sentences and everyday words. Avoid empty words such as 'passionate' or 'expert' unless your samples prove them.

cards.question: Which headline is strongest for Ayesha?
options: Creative, passionate and hard-working designer
Social media post design for small food businesses
Designer | Writer | Editor | Data entry | More
cards.explanation: It names the service and the client clearly. The others describe personality or list unrelated skills.

cards.title: Set up your first gig
cards.prompt: Put the main steps of creating a gig in a sensible order. Field names differ by platform.
steps: Write a clear title that names the result
Choose the closest category for your service
Set packages with what is included and the delivery time
Write a description that explains the result, process and what you need
Add honest images or samples of your own work
List the information the buyer must send before you start

cards.title: A weak proposal and a strong proposal
cards.caption: A strong proposal is short and about the client's job, not a copied speech about yourself.

items.label: Opening
items.right: Repeats the client's goal in one line

items.label: Focus
items.right: How you will solve this job

items.label: Proof
items.right: One or two matching samples

items.label: Questions
items.right: One smart question about the job

items.label: Length
items.right: Short, specific and tailored

cards.title: Bilal's first tailored proposal
cards.body:
A small shoe shop in Peshawar posted: 'Need a simple website to show our products and location. Must work well on phones.' Bilal wrote:

> Hello, you need a simple, phone-friendly website that shows your shoes and helps customers find your shop.
>
> I recently built a similar site for a clothing shop (link) with a product gallery, a map and a WhatsApp contact button.
>
> My plan: a home page, a product gallery you can update yourself, and a contact page with your map. I can share a first version for your feedback before finishing.
>
> One question: do you already have product photos, or would you like advice on taking them with a phone?

It is short, repeats the client's need, shows proof and ends with a useful question.

cards.title: Strong or weak profile element?
cards.prompt: Sort each element of a beginner's profile.

items.text: Samples created by the freelancer, labelled as practice projects
Designs copied from someone else's portfolio
A clear photo and a headline that names the service
Claiming 'ten years of experience' when you have one
A short list of what is included in each package
Spelling mistakes throughout the overview
Real languages listed at your honest level

cards.title: No clients, no portfolio
cards.situation: Ayesha has no paid clients yet, so her portfolio is empty. A friend suggests downloading attractive designs from the internet and adding them to her profile 'just to start'. What should she do?

choices.text: Create three practice posts for imaginary or local businesses, label them as sample projects and add them.
choices.outcome: Best choice. Honest samples show her real skill, and labelling them avoids misleading clients. She can replace them with client work later.

choices.text: Use the downloaded designs because everyone does it.
choices.outcome: This is copying someone else's work. It is dishonest, may break copyright and platform rules, and she will not be able to deliver the same quality on demand.

choices.text: Offer to design posts for a relative's shop for free in return for permission to show the work.
choices.outcome: Acceptable. Real work for a real business, shown with permission, is a good start, though she should still label it honestly and not treat it as a paid review.

choices.text: Leave the portfolio empty and wait until a client hires her.
choices.outcome: Clients rarely hire without seeing any samples, so this may mean a long wait.

cards.question: A first proposal should mainly show the client that…
options: You understand their job and can solve it
You have the longest list of skills on the site
You will accept any price they choose
You have written the same proposal many times
cards.explanation: Clients want to know you understood their need. Tailored, specific proposals stand out from copied ones.

cards.title: Parts of a strong proposal
cards.prompt: Match each part to what it does.

pairs.right: Shows you read the job by restating the client's goal
Proves you have done similar work
Explains how you will tackle this job
Starts a conversation and shows careful thinking

cards.title: Use AI and templates honestly
cards.body: AI tools can help you check grammar or plan a proposal, but the final words must be true and fit the job. Never claim work, reviews or qualifications that are not yours. Do not paste a client's private files into tools without permission. Honesty from the first message protects your reviews and your account.

cards.title: Take-aways from the Shop Window
items: Your profile is a shop window: photo, headline and first lines must show what you do and for whom.
Write about the client's problem and result, using short sentences and everyday words.
With no clients yet, create honest, labelled sample projects of your own.
A first gig needs a clear title, packages, a helpful description, honest images and buyer requirements.
A strong proposal is short, tailored, shows one or two relevant samples and asks one smart question.

cards.prompt: Rewrite your headline so that it names your service and your client. Then write the first two lines of a proposal for a real job you could do. Do they talk about the client's need, or about you?

quiz.question: What should a profile headline do?
options: Describe your personality using several strong, impressive adjectives
Name your service and the kind of client you serve
List every tool and skill you have ever used
Tell clients your full education history
quiz.explanation: A clear headline tells clients in seconds whether you can help with their kind of problem.

quiz.question: Which opening line is most client-focused?
options: I am a passionate designer who loves colours
Dear Sir, I am an expert in all kinds of design
Please check my profile for more details
You need posts that make your dishes look delicious online
quiz.explanation: It starts from the client's need and result, which is what the client cares about.

quiz.question: Ayesha has no clients yet. What is the honest way to build a portfolio?
options: Create her own sample projects and label them as samples
Download attractive designs and show them as her own
Copy a well-known designer's whole portfolio layout and images
Leave the portfolio empty and add fake client names
quiz.explanation: Labelled practice projects show real skill without misleading anyone. Copying others' work is dishonest and can break copyright and platform rules.

quiz.question: In a gig, what is the purpose of listing buyer requirements?
options: To make the gig look longer and more serious
To ask the buyer for their account password
To collect the information you need before starting
To raise the price of the gig automatically for every new order
quiz.explanation: Clear requirements, such as logo files, text or photos, help you start quickly and avoid misunderstandings. Never ask for passwords.

quiz.question: What usually makes a proposal weak?
options: A long, copied message about yourself that ignores the job
Restating the client's goal in the first line
Including one relevant work sample
Asking one thoughtful question about the project
quiz.explanation: Copied, self-focused proposals show the client you did not read their job. Tailored ones stand out.

quiz.question: Bilal's proposal ends with 'Do you already have product photos?' Why is this a good ending?
options: It proves he has many years of experience
It starts a conversation and shows he thought about the job
It forces the client to hire him immediately
It lets him avoid writing a plan for the work
quiz.explanation: A smart question invites a reply and shows care. It also uncovers needs that affect scope and price.

quiz.question: Which claim on a beginner's profile is a problem?
options: Listing Urdu and English on the profile at an honest, real level
Labelling practice projects as sample work
Saying 'ten years of experience' when it is one year
Adding a clear, friendly profile photo
quiz.explanation: False claims mislead clients and break trust when the truth appears. They can also break platform rules.

quiz.question: Ayesha uses an AI tool to check the grammar of her proposal. What must she still make sure of?
options: The proposal is as long as possible
The proposal mentions as many tools as possible
The client's private files are pasted into the tool
Every statement is true and fits this specific job
quiz.explanation: Tools can help with wording, but she is responsible for honesty and fit. Clients' private files should not go into tools without permission.

quiz.question: What is the best order for a simple client-focused overview?
options: Your hobbies, your school, your city, your age
Your prices, your rules, your fees, your hours
A long list of skills first, then a polite request for some reviews
Client's need, what you do, how you work, an invitation
quiz.explanation: This structure keeps the focus on the client and ends with an easy next step.

quiz.question: Why are two or three matching samples better than many unrelated ones?
options: They show clearly that you can do this client's kind of work
Platforms only allow three files on any profile
Clients never look at more than one sample
Unrelated samples are always against the rules
quiz.explanation: Matching samples prove the exact skill the client is hiring for and keep your profile focused.

sessions.title: Winning Clients: Proposals, Pricing, Communication and Reviews
sessions.summary: Move from sending proposals to winning contracts: diagnose why proposals fail, price your work with a clear method instead of guessing, handle price pressure calmly, communicate like a professional and earn honest reviews that bring the next client.
objectives: Use a repeatable structure to write proposals that win replies
Set prices using your costs, the value to the client and the market, and choose hourly or fixed pricing
Respond to price pressure by adjusting scope, not by cutting your rate blindly
Communicate clearly and on time before, during and after a project
Earn and respond to reviews honestly and professionally

cards.title: Forty proposals, two replies
cards.setting: Kamran's small office in Islamabad. Bilal visits during a trip, laptop open.

lines.text: I have sent forty proposals. Two replies. Both said my price was too high. Should I just work for almost nothing?
Show me five of your proposals. And tell me how you chose your price.
I copied the same message each time. And the price… I saw what others charge and went a bit lower.
Then the problem is not only price. Clients cannot see why you are the right person. And your price has no method behind it.
(on speaker from Faisalabad) As a client, I pay more for someone who understands my shop and replies clearly. Cheap is expensive if I must redo it.
Welcome to Premium, Bilal. Today we build a proposal system and a pricing method you can defend.

cards.title: The proposal that gets a reply

scenes.heading: Hook with their goal
scenes.narration: Your first line appears in the client's list of proposals. Restate their goal or problem in their own words so they know you read the job.

scenes.heading: Show you understand
scenes.narration: Add one insight: a risk you spotted, a better approach or a question that matters. This is where you stand out from copied messages.

scenes.heading: Prove it
scenes.narration: Link one or two samples that closely match. If you have none, describe a short plan in clear steps.

scenes.heading: Plan and price
scenes.narration: Give a simple plan, a timeline you can meet and a price with what it includes. Make it easy to compare.

scenes.heading: Call to action
scenes.narration: End with a question or a simple next step, such as a short call or a first draft by a set day.

cards.title: From proposals to repeat clients
cards.caption: Track each stage in a simple sheet. If one stage is weak, fix that stage instead of only sending more proposals.

items.label: Proposals sent
items.detail: Choose jobs that truly fit your service. Fewer, better proposals beat many copied ones.

items.label: Client views
items.detail: A strong first line and good fit make clients open your proposal.

items.label: Replies and interviews
items.detail: Tailored insight and matching samples get conversations started.

items.label: Contracts won
items.detail: Clear plan, fair price and quick, polite answers turn talks into work.

items.label: Repeat clients
items.detail: Excellent delivery and communication bring clients back.

cards.title: Pricing with a method
cards.body:
Guessing a price, or always going lower than others, leads to tired freelancers and doubtful clients. Use three views:

- **Your floor:** what you need to cover your time, internet, electricity, software and savings. Below this you lose money.
- **The value to the client:** a website that brings orders, or a menu that helps a café sell, is worth more to the client than an hour of your time.
- **The market:** what similar freelancers with similar reviews offer. Use it as a guide, not a rule.

As a beginner you may start near your floor to earn reviews, but raise your prices step by step as your reviews and skills grow. Platform fees and payment charges also reduce what you receive, so check the current terms and include them in your calculation.

cards.title: Hourly or fixed price?
cards.caption: Many freelancers use both. Platforms offer different contract types and rules, so check the current options.

items.label: Best for
items.right: Clear, well-defined projects

items.label: Client sees
items.right: One total for agreed results

items.label: Your risk
items.right: Higher if scope is vague

items.label: You must
items.right: Define scope and revisions clearly

items.label: Reward for speed
items.right: More, since you keep the same price

cards.question: Bilal is asked to 'improve an old website, fix whatever is broken and add some features'. The work is unclear. Which pricing is usually safer for him?
options: A low fixed price for the whole job so he wins it
Hourly, or a small paid first step to clarify scope
Working free until the client decides what they want
cards.explanation: When scope is unclear, hourly work or a small paid discovery step protects him. A vague fixed-price job can grow far beyond the price.

cards.title: Ayesha works out her floor price
cards.body:
These numbers are only an example for practice, not a guide to market rates.

Ayesha wants to earn **Rs 40,000** in a month from freelancing. She has about **80 hours** a month, but only around **half** goes into paid work; the rest goes into proposals, messages and learning. So she has about **40 paid hours**.

Rs 40,000 ÷ 40 hours = **Rs 1,000 per paid hour** before costs and fees.

A social media post takes her about **2 hours** including one revision, so her floor is about **Rs 2,000 per post**, plus a margin for internet, software, platform fees and payment charges.

Now she compares with the market and the value to the client, and sets packages above her floor.

cards.title: Professional or unprofessional communication?
cards.prompt: Sort each message habit.

items.text: Replying within a reasonable time, even just to say when you will answer fully
Confirming the agreed scope and deadline in writing
Going silent for days, then delivering late without warning
Sending ten voice notes instead of one clear written summary
Telling the client early if a delay is likely, with a new date
Arguing angrily when the client asks a question
Sharing a short progress update at an agreed point

cards.title: 'Too expensive. Do it for half.'
cards.situation: A clothing shop owner in Karachi likes Ayesha's samples and wants ten posts for a sale. Her quote was fair and above her floor. The client replies: 'Too expensive. Another designer will do it for half. Can you match?'

choices.text: Thank the client, explain what the price includes, and offer a smaller package, such as five posts, that fits their budget.
choices.outcome: Best choice. She protects her rate and still helps the client by adjusting the scope rather than her value.

choices.text: Cut her price by half to win the job.
choices.outcome: She may win this job, but she will work below her floor and the client learns that her prices are not serious.

choices.text: Reply that the other designer must be bad and refuse to discuss.
choices.outcome: Unprofessional. Criticising others or ending the talk rudely damages her reputation.

choices.text: Offer a small discount for a repeat order next month.
choices.outcome: Acceptable. A modest, planned discount for repeat work can be fair, as long as it stays above her floor.

cards.back: 'To confirm: ten posts, two rounds of changes, delivery by Friday. Please send your logo and photos.'
'Quick update: the first five designs are ready for your feedback.'
'I need one extra day to finish properly. New delivery: Saturday afternoon. Sorry for the change.'
'Your files are attached in the formats we agreed. Let me know if any changes are needed.'
'Thank you for working with me. If you are happy, a review would really help my small business.'

cards.title: Reviews: what to do
cards.prompt: Match each situation to the professional response.

pairs.right: Thank them and politely ask for honest feedback

pairs.left: Client offers five stars for a discount
pairs.right: Decline; reviews must be honest, not bought
Reply calmly, thank them and say what you will improve
Reply briefly with facts and use the platform's support process

cards.question: Which is the best way to ask for a review?
options: Offer a discount only if they leave five stars
After approval, thank them and ask for honest feedback
Ask a friend to leave reviews while you wait
Refuse to deliver files until they write a review
cards.explanation: Asking politely for honest feedback after a good delivery is professional. Buying, faking or forcing reviews is dishonest and usually against platform rules.

cards.title: From proposal to five-star experience
cards.prompt: Put the steps in order.
steps: Choose a job that truly fits your service
Send a short, tailored proposal with matching proof
Agree the scope, price and deadline in writing
Share progress and deliver on time
Make the agreed revisions and confirm approval
Thank the client and ask for honest feedback

cards.title: Take-aways from the Pitch Room
items: Track your funnel: if replies are low, fix your first line and fit before sending more proposals.
Price with a method: your floor, the value to the client and the market, plus fees you must check.
Use hourly or a paid first step when scope is unclear; use fixed price when it is well defined.
Under price pressure, change the scope, not your value.
Communicate early and in writing, and ask for honest reviews; never buy or fake them.

cards.prompt: Work out your own floor price using your monthly goal and your real paid hours. Then write a short, polite reply to a client who says your price is too high, offering a smaller scope instead of a lower rate.

quiz.question: Bilal sent many copied proposals and got almost no replies. What should he fix first?
options: The colour scheme of his profile photo
The number of proposals he sends each day
The fit and first lines of his proposals
The length of his skills list
quiz.explanation: If clients do not reply, the proposal itself is the weak stage. Tailored first lines and better job fit usually help more than sending more copies.

quiz.question: What is your 'floor price'?
options: The highest price any client has ever paid
The lowest price that still covers your time and costs
The average price shown for a service on a platform's home page
The fee a platform charges for every order
quiz.explanation: Below your floor you lose money. It is based on your income goal, your real paid hours and your costs.

quiz.question: Ayesha's monthly goal is Rs 30,000 and she has about 30 paid hours a month. Before costs and fees, what is her hourly floor?
options: Rs 300 per hour
Rs 3,000 per hour
Rs 10,000 per hour
Rs 1,000 per hour
quiz.explanation: Rs 30,000 divided by 30 paid hours is Rs 1,000 per hour, before adding costs, fees and margin. This is a practice calculation only.

quiz.question: When is a fixed-price contract usually a good choice?
options: When the scope and results are clearly defined
When the client cannot yet explain what they need
When the work is ongoing with no clear end
When no one has agreed the number of revisions
quiz.explanation: Fixed price works when both sides know exactly what will be delivered. Unclear work is safer hourly or with a paid first step.

quiz.question: A client says, 'Too expensive, do it for half.' What is the most professional response?
options: Cut the price in half immediately to win the job
Explain what is included and offer a smaller scope that fits
Tell the client that the other, cheaper freelancer must be poor quality
Stop replying to the client without any explanation
quiz.explanation: Adjusting scope keeps your rate fair and still helps the client. Price cuts below your floor hurt your business.

quiz.question: Which message is best when a delay becomes likely?
options: Saying nothing and delivering late without warning
Delivering unfinished work on time without comment
Telling the client early, with a new realistic date
Blaming the client for sending files late in every case
quiz.explanation: Early, honest updates keep trust. Silence and surprises damage it.

quiz.question: A client offers five stars if Ayesha gives a big discount. What should she do?
options: Politely decline and keep her normal, honest process
Accept, because five stars help her ranking
Accept, but ask for the review to be very long
Ask the client to write the review from another account
quiz.explanation: Trading discounts for ratings is not honest feedback and usually breaks platform rules.

quiz.question: Why should platform fees and payment charges be part of your pricing?
options: They are always paid entirely by the client
They are the same on every platform forever
They only apply to clients in other countries
They reduce what you actually receive from each project
quiz.explanation: Fees and charges vary by platform and payment method and change over time. Check the current terms and include them in your numbers.

quiz.question: A client leaves a fair review saying communication was slow. How should you reply?
options: Argue publicly that the client was the real problem
Ask the platform to delete every critical review
Thank them calmly and explain how you will improve
Ignore it and open a new account with no reviews
quiz.explanation: A calm, constructive reply shows future clients that you take feedback seriously.

quiz.question: In the proposal funnel, many clients view Bilal's proposals but few reply. Which stage is weakest?
options: Choosing jobs that fit his service
Turning views into replies with insight and proof
Delivering finished work on time
Bringing his past clients back again for more repeat work
quiz.explanation: Views show the first line works; low replies suggest the body lacks tailored insight, matching samples or a clear next step.

sessions.title: Delivering Professionally: Scope, Revisions, Agreements and Difficult Clients
sessions.summary: Deliver like a professional: agree a clear scope and revision policy in writing, handle change requests without losing money or goodwill, manage your time across several clients, and stay calm and fair with difficult clients using the platform's processes when needed.
objectives: Write a clear scope with deliverables, revisions, deadlines and client inputs
Handle change requests and scope creep with a simple, polite process
Use written agreements and platform contracts in general terms, and know when to seek advice
Plan time across several projects so you deliver on time
Respond to difficult clients calmly and use dispute processes fairly

cards.title: Just one more small change
cards.setting: Nasreen's pickle kitchen and office, Faisalabad. Ayesha is designing her new label.

lines.text: The label is lovely! Now, can you also make a version for the big jar? And one for Instagram. And maybe a small flyer?
(to herself) This is the fourth 'small change'. We agreed one label and two rounds of changes. I have done six.
(later, to Kamran) I do not want to upset her. She is a kind client. But I am working for free now.
This is called scope creep. It is nobody's villain story. It happens when the scope is not clear, or when we do not speak up early.
Professionals agree the scope in writing and treat new requests as new work, politely. Let us fix this the right way.

cards.title: Scope and revisions in plain words

scenes.heading: Scope
scenes.narration: The scope is the list of exactly what you will deliver: what, how many, which formats and by when. If it is not in the scope, it is not included.

scenes.heading: Revisions
scenes.narration: A revision is a change to work you delivered, inside the agreed scope. Decide in advance how many rounds are included and what counts as a revision.

scenes.heading: Change request
scenes.narration: A new item, a new size or a new idea is not a revision. It is a change request, and it can have a new price and deadline.

scenes.heading: Write it down
scenes.narration: Confirm the scope, revisions, price and deadline in writing, on the platform where possible. A clear record helps everyone if memories differ later.

cards.title: A professional project workflow
cards.caption: Use this for every project, large or small. It prevents most misunderstandings.

items.label: Brief
items.detail: Ask questions and understand the goal, audience and must-haves.

items.label: Scope in writing
items.detail: Deliverables, formats, revisions, deadline, price and client inputs.

items.label: First draft
items.detail: Share early work at the agreed point for direction.

items.label: Agreed revisions
items.detail: Make the included rounds of changes.

items.label: Final delivery
items.detail: Deliver the agreed files through the agreed channel.

items.label: Handover and close
items.detail: Confirm approval, share any instructions and thank the client.

cards.title: Agreements and contracts, in general terms
cards.body:
On a marketplace, the order or contract and the platform's terms set the basic rules. Add the details in the order or the messages: deliverables, revisions, deadlines and what the client must provide.

With direct clients outside a marketplace, use a **short written agreement**, such as an e-mail both sides confirm, covering:

- The work, deliverables and formats
- Price, payment timing and method
- Number of revisions and how extra work is priced
- Deadlines and what happens if inputs arrive late
- Who owns or may use the final work, and when

This is general guidance, not legal advice. For large or unusual projects, or work for clients in other countries, check the law that applies and consider advice from a qualified professional.

cards.question: Nasreen asks Ayesha for a new flyer after the label is approved. What is this?
options: A normal revision that is already included
A change request that can have its own price and deadline
A reason to stop working with Nasreen at once
cards.explanation: A new item outside the agreed scope is a change request. Ayesha can quote it separately and politely.

cards.title: Revision or change request?
cards.prompt: The agreed scope is one product label with two rounds of changes. Sort each request.

items.text: Make the brand name a little larger
Change the background to the darker green
Design a second label for a new product
Create an Instagram post using the label
Fix a spelling mistake in the ingredients list
Make a printed flyer for a food fair

cards.title: Plan your week across clients
cards.caption: Put each task in a box. Do urgent and important work first, schedule important work before it becomes urgent, and keep low-value tasks small.

items.label: Do now
items.detail: Urgent and important: tomorrow's delivery, a client waiting on a fix.

items.label: Schedule
items.detail: Important, not urgent: samples, learning, next week's project.

items.label: Do quickly
items.detail: Urgent, less important: short admin replies; keep them brief.

items.label: Limit
items.detail: Neither: endless scrolling, redesigning your profile again and again.

cards.title: The angry message at midnight
cards.situation: A client from a different time zone writes in capital letters: 'THIS IS NOT WHAT I WANTED. I WANT UNLIMITED CHANGES OR A FULL REFUND.' Bilal delivered exactly what was agreed in the written scope, on time.

choices.text: Wait until he is calm, reply politely, refer to the agreed scope, ask what exactly is wrong and offer the included revision.
choices.outcome: Best choice. He stays professional, focuses on facts and gives the client a fair way forward. If it cannot be solved, he can use the platform's resolution process.

choices.text: Reply immediately in capital letters, defending himself.
choices.outcome: Matching anger rarely solves anything and a written record of rudeness can hurt him in a dispute.

choices.text: Agree to unlimited changes to avoid a bad review.
choices.outcome: This feels safe, but he will work far beyond the price, and it teaches the client that pressure works.

choices.text: Offer one extra goodwill change as a gesture, while clearly restating the agreed scope.
choices.outcome: Acceptable. A small, limited gesture can rescue a relationship if it does not set a habit of free work.

cards.back: Ask specific questions and share examples to choose from. Confirm answers in writing.
Send a polite reminder with the date you need inputs, and explain how delays move the deadline.
Refer to the agreed revisions and quote extra rounds as new work.
Stay calm and factual, never insult back, and use platform support if needed.
Keep to the platform's payment process or your written payment terms before delivering final files.

cards.title: Handle a change request politely
cards.prompt: Put the steps in order.
steps: Thank the client for the new idea
Explain kindly that it is outside the agreed scope
Give a clear price and delivery time for the extra work
Wait for the client to agree in writing
Add the new work through the platform's process or your agreement
Deliver it with the same care as the original work

cards.question: Ayesha has three deliveries this week and one client asks for a call at short notice about a future project. Using the time-planning grid, what is the best approach?
options: Drop everything to take the call right now
Finish urgent deliveries first and offer a call time later this week
Ignore the request because it is not urgent
Cancel one delivery to make time for the call
cards.explanation: A future project is important but not urgent. Scheduling it protects her current deadlines and still respects the new client.

cards.title: Use the platform's processes
cards.body: If a disagreement cannot be solved by calm messages, use the platform's official resolution or support process instead of threats. Keep all key messages and files on the platform, deliver through its delivery tools and save your drafts. Processes and protections differ by platform and contract type, so read the current help pages.

cards.title: Delivery words
cards.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.

pairs.right: A specific piece of work you hand over, such as a logo file
Extra work slowly added without changing price or deadline
One set of changes to delivered work inside the scope
Things the client must provide, such as text, logos or access
Final step: delivering files and any instructions to close the project

cards.title: Take-aways from the Workshop
items: Agree scope, revisions, deadline, price and client inputs in writing before you start.
A revision changes delivered work inside the scope; a new item is a change request with its own price.
Use short written agreements with direct clients and seek qualified advice for large or unusual work.
Plan your week by urgency and importance so current deadlines are protected.
With difficult clients, stay calm and factual and use the platform's processes when needed.

cards.prompt: Think of a project you have done or might do. Write its scope in five lines: deliverables, formats, revisions, deadline and client inputs. Then write one polite sentence you could use when a client asks for something outside it.

quiz.question: What does a project's scope describe?
options: How many hours you spent learning your skill
The list of all clients you have worked with
Your own personal opinion of the client's business and its products
Exactly what you will deliver, in what form and by when
quiz.explanation: Scope sets the boundaries of the project, so both sides know what is and is not included.

quiz.question: The agreed scope is one logo with two revision rounds. The client asks for a matching business card. What is this?
options: A change request outside the scope
The second included revision round
A spelling correction inside the scope
A normal part of every logo project
quiz.explanation: A new item is new work. It can be quoted with its own price and deadline.

quiz.question: What is 'scope creep'?
options: A client paying the freelancer earlier than was agreed in the contract
A freelancer finishing a project ahead of schedule
Extra work added bit by bit without changing price or deadline
A platform changing its search results each week
quiz.explanation: Scope creep slowly turns a fair project into unpaid work. Clear scope and polite change requests prevent it.

quiz.question: With a direct client outside a marketplace, what is a sensible minimum agreement?
options: A verbal promise in a voice note that is later deleted
A written note both sides confirm, covering work, price, revisions and deadlines
Nothing, because trust is enough between good people
A copy of the platform's terms from another website
quiz.explanation: A short written agreement prevents most disputes. For large or unusual work, seek qualified advice.

quiz.question: A client sends an angry message demanding unlimited changes, although Bilal delivered the agreed scope on time. What should he do first?
options: Reply calmly, refer to the scope and ask what exactly needs changing
Reply instantly in the same angry tone
Agree to unlimited changes to avoid any risk
Delete the conversation and stop replying
quiz.explanation: Calm, factual replies focused on the agreement give the best chance of a fair outcome and leave a good record.

quiz.question: On the urgency and importance grid, where does 'build new samples for next month' belong?
options: Urgent and important: do it right now
Urgent but less important: do it quickly
Neither urgent nor important: drop it
Important but not urgent: schedule it
quiz.explanation: Samples matter for growth but rarely have a deadline today, so plan a fixed time for them.

quiz.question: A disagreement with a marketplace client cannot be solved by messages. What is the professional next step?
options: Post the client's name and personal details on social media as a warning
Use the platform's official resolution or support process
Threaten the client with a bad review in return
Open a new account and start again elsewhere
quiz.explanation: Platforms have processes for disputes. Using them, with your messages and files on record, is fair and professional.

quiz.question: Which item is a client input?
options: The final logo file you hand over at the end
The second round of changes you make
The product photos the client must send before work starts
Your own estimate of the total hours needed
quiz.explanation: Client inputs are what the client provides. Late inputs can move the deadline, which your agreement should say.

quiz.question: Ayesha is unsure who may use a design after a project for a client in another country. What is the sensible approach?
options: Agree usage in writing and check the law or take advice for unusual cases
Assume she can always resell the design to anyone
Assume the client owns everything she has ever made
Avoid the topic because it is too complicated
quiz.explanation: Ownership and usage should be agreed in writing. Laws differ by country, so check the law that applies or seek qualified advice when unsure.

quiz.question: Why should you deliver files through the platform's delivery tool on marketplace projects?
options: It makes the files open faster on every device
It automatically doubles the price of the order
It keeps a clear record and follows the platform's payment process
It lets you skip the agreed revision rounds
quiz.explanation: Delivering on-platform creates a record and links the delivery to the platform's process and protection, which depend on its current terms.

sessions.title: Growing a Freelance Business: Payments, Records, Safety and Your Brand
sessions.summary: Run freelancing as a real business: understand in general terms how international payments reach you, keep simple records and take tax duties seriously, spot and avoid scams aimed at freelancers, protect your accounts, and grow through repeat clients and a trusted personal brand.
objectives: Describe in general terms how freelancers in Pakistan receive international payments, and why to check current terms and the law
Keep simple income and expense records and understand tax duties in general terms
Recognise common scams aimed at freelancers and respond safely
Protect your accounts and clients' data
Build repeat clients and a personal brand that brings work to you

cards.title: Money in, questions out
cards.setting: A café in Islamabad. Bilal and Ayesha meet Kamran after six months of freelancing.

lines.text: I have regular clients now! But payments come in different ways and I have no idea what to do about taxes.
And yesterday someone sent me a 'job' asking me to pay a registration fee first. It looked so real.
Both of you have reached the stage where freelancing becomes a business. Businesses need three things: clean money, safe accounts and a good name.
(joining the table) And clients who come back. I keep going back to Ayesha because she is reliable and easy to work with.
Exactly. Today: getting paid safely, keeping records, avoiding scams and building a brand that brings people like Nasreen back.

cards.title: Getting paid from abroad, in general terms

scenes.heading: Many routes
scenes.narration: Money usually travels from the client to the platform, then to you through a withdrawal method, such as a bank transfer or a payment service account. Direct clients may pay by bank transfer or a payment service.

scenes.heading: Official channels
scenes.narration: Receive foreign payments through proper, legal banking and payment channels in your own name. Avoid informal routes or using someone else's account.

scenes.heading: Methods and rules vary
scenes.narration: Which methods are available, their charges, exchange rates and processing times vary by platform, provider and country, and they change. Check the current terms of each provider.

scenes.heading: Follow the law
scenes.narration: Banking, foreign exchange and tax rules apply to freelance income. They can change, so check current official guidance from the State Bank, the FBR and your bank, or ask a qualified adviser.

scenes.heading: Keep proof
scenes.narration: Save invoices, platform statements and bank records for every payment. Banks or tax authorities may ask you to show where money came from.

cards.title: How a payment usually reaches you
cards.caption: A general picture only. Steps, charges and timings differ by platform and provider; check their current terms.

items.label: Client pays
items.detail: Through the platform, or by an agreed method for direct clients.

items.label: Funds become available
items.detail: The platform releases funds under its own process and timing.

items.label: You withdraw
items.detail: To a method in your own name that the platform supports.

items.label: Money arrives in your account
items.detail: Possibly converted to rupees, with any charges shown.

items.label: You record it
items.detail: Save the statement and note the amount in your records.

cards.title: Records and taxes, in general terms
cards.body:
Freelance income is business income. Keep a simple record from the first rupee:

- **Income:** date, client, project, amount, platform or method, and any fees deducted.
- **Expenses:** internet, software, equipment and other business costs, with receipts.
- **Documents:** invoices, platform statements and bank statements, saved in one folder each month.

Tax rules for freelancers, including how foreign income is treated and whether you need to register or file a return, are set by law and can change. Do not rely on rumours. Check current guidance from the **FBR (Federal Board of Revenue)**, ask your bank what documents it needs, and consider a qualified tax adviser as your income grows. Good records make all of this much easier.

cards.question: Bilal hears from a friend that 'freelancers never need to think about tax'. What should he do?
options: Believe it and stop keeping any records
Keep records and check current official guidance or an adviser
Move his income into a relative's account to be safe
cards.explanation: Tax rules are set by law and can change. Records plus current official guidance or qualified advice are the safe approach. Using someone else's account creates more risk.

cards.title: Scam red flag or normal client behaviour?
cards.prompt: Sort each message Ayesha receives.

items.text: 'Pay a registration fee and we will send you high-paying work'
'I sent too much money by mistake, please refund the extra outside the platform'
'Install this file to see the project brief'
'Please share your account login so my team can upload files'
'Could you send two samples similar to this style?'
'What is your delivery time for ten posts?'
'Can we start through the platform with a small first order?'

cards.title: The repeat-client cycle
cards.caption: Winning a new client takes much more effort than keeping a happy one. Make every project lead to the next.

items.label: Deliver excellent work
items.detail: On time, inside scope, with clear communication.

items.label: Make it easy
items.detail: Organised files, simple instructions and friendly handover.

items.label: Stay in touch
items.detail: A short, useful check-in later, without spamming.

items.label: Suggest the next step
items.detail: Offer a related service that helps their business.

items.label: Earn referrals
items.detail: Happy clients recommend you to others.

cards.title: The payment that is 'too much'
cards.situation: A new direct client, not on any platform, says he will send Bilal a large payment for a website, much more than the quote. He then asks Bilal to send the 'extra' to his 'designer friend' quickly by mobile wallet before the payment has fully cleared.

choices.text: Refuse to send any money, explain he only accepts the agreed amount through a verified method, and stop if the client insists.
choices.outcome: Best choice. This is a classic overpayment scam: the first payment can be reversed later, and the money he sent is gone.

choices.text: Send the extra quickly so the client stays happy.
choices.outcome: This is exactly what scammers want. If the original payment fails or is reversed, Bilal loses his own money.

choices.text: Wait until the money appears in his account, then send the extra.
choices.outcome: Still risky. Money can appear and later be reversed. He should never forward 'extra' money for a stranger.

choices.text: Ask the client to pay only the agreed amount through a platform instead.
choices.outcome: A good safe alternative. If the client refuses, that is another warning sign.

cards.title: Building blocks of a personal brand

cards.back: Be known for one main thing, such as 'phone-friendly websites for small shops'.
Show the problem, what you did and the result, with the client's permission.
Share short tips on LinkedIn or social media that help your ideal clients.
Use the same photo, name and description everywhere clients may find you.
Honest reviews, kept promises and good manners are the heart of your brand.

cards.title: Which record is this?
cards.prompt: Match each record to what it shows.

pairs.right: A bill showing the work, amount and payment terms for a client
A list of earnings, fees and withdrawals on the platform
Proof of money received into your own account
Proof of a business cost such as software or internet

cards.question: Which habit best protects Ayesha's freelance accounts?
options: Sharing her login with clients who ask politely
Turning on two-step verification and keeping her login private
Using the same simple password for every website
Letting a friend run her account while she studies
cards.explanation: Two-step verification and a private login protect your income and reputation. Sharing accounts or letting others use them usually breaks platform rules and invites fraud.

cards.title: A simple monthly money routine
cards.prompt: Put the steps in order.
steps: Download the month's platform and bank statements
Record each payment with client, project, fees and amount
Add business expenses and save the receipts
Set aside money for savings and possible tax
Check current official guidance or your adviser on any new questions

cards.title: Guard your accounts and your clients
cards.body: Use strong, different passwords and two-step verification. Never share your login, never let anyone else work from your account, and never open unknown files that 'contain the brief'. Keep client files private, delete them when no longer needed under your agreement, and do not put clients' private data into AI or other tools without permission.

cards.title: Take-aways from the Growth Road
items: Receive payments through legal channels in your own name; methods, charges and rules vary and change, so check current terms and the law.
Keep monthly records of income, fees and expenses, and check current FBR guidance or a qualified adviser on tax.
Red flags: fees to get work, overpayment refunds, unknown files, requests for your login, and moving off-platform fast.
Protect accounts with strong passwords and two-step verification, and keep client data private.
Grow through repeat clients, referrals and a focused, honest personal brand.

cards.prompt: Set up your own simple record sheet with columns for date, client, project, amount, fees and method. Then write the one-line focus of your personal brand, and name one past or future client you could help again with a related service.

quiz.question: What is the safest general way to receive international freelance payments?
options: Through a relative's account to avoid any questions
Through legal banking or payment channels in your own name
In cash from strangers who visit your home
Through any informal route that offers a slightly better exchange rate
quiz.explanation: Legal channels in your own name protect you and keep a clear record. Methods and rules vary, so check current terms and the law.

quiz.question: Why should you check current terms before choosing a withdrawal or payment method?
options: Every method is free and instant everywhere
All platforms support exactly the same methods
Payment methods never change once you start
Availability, charges and timings vary by provider and change
quiz.explanation: Methods, charges, exchange rates and timings differ and change, so check each provider's current terms.

quiz.question: Which records should a freelancer keep for each payment?
options: Date, client, project, amount, fees and the method used
Only the client's star rating for the project
Only the total for the year, from memory
Nothing at all, because the platform keeps every record for you anyway
quiz.explanation: Clear records make tax, bank questions and planning much easier.

quiz.question: Bilal is unsure whether he must register or file a tax return for freelance income. What should he do?
options: Follow a rumour he heard in a group chat
Assume freelance income is never taxed
Check current FBR guidance or ask a qualified tax adviser
Hide the income in a friend's account
quiz.explanation: Tax rules are set by law and can change. Official guidance or a qualified adviser is the reliable source.

quiz.question: A 'client' asks Ayesha to pay a registration fee before sending work. What is this most likely?
options: A normal requirement on every marketplace
A tax she must pay to the government
A standard deposit for all design work
A scam aimed at freelancers
quiz.explanation: Genuine clients pay you for work; they do not charge you for the chance to work. Fees to get work are a classic red flag.

quiz.question: A new client overpays and asks Bilal to forward the extra to a friend before the payment fully clears. Why is this dangerous?
options: It will make his delivery time slightly longer
The original payment can be reversed, and his money is lost
It could make his invoice and project records look less professional
It means the client might leave a short review
quiz.explanation: This is an overpayment scam. Never forward 'extra' money for a stranger; accept only the agreed amount through a verified method.

quiz.question: Which habit best protects your freelance account?
options: Two-step verification and never sharing your login
Using one simple password for every site
Letting a trusted friend work from your account when you are busy
Saving your password in your public profile
quiz.explanation: Account security protects your income and reviews. Sharing or renting accounts usually breaks platform rules.

quiz.question: Why is keeping a happy client often better value than finding a new one?
options: Repeat clients are never allowed to leave reviews
New clients always pay less than old clients
Platforms ban freelancers who only ever work with brand-new clients
Repeat clients already trust you, so winning work takes less effort
quiz.explanation: Trust is already built, so repeat work and referrals come more easily.

quiz.question: What should a strong portfolio case study include?
options: The client's private files and contact details
Only a list of software you used
The client's problem, what you did and the result, with permission
Your prices and the platform's current fees
quiz.explanation: Case studies show your thinking and results. Always get permission and keep private details out.

quiz.question: A stranger sends a file saying 'open this to see the project brief' and asks you to install it. What should you do?
options: Open it quickly so you do not lose the client
Do not open or install it; ask for the brief as text on the platform
Install it, then share your login so they can check
Forward it to all your clients to ask their opinion
quiz.explanation: Unknown files are a common way to steal accounts and data. Genuine clients can describe the job in a message.

bank.question: A student can write, design, edit video and do data entry, but has strong samples only in design. Which first service is most sensible?
options: All four services, to appear in more searches
A focused design service for one type of client
Video editing, because it seems to be in fashion
Data entry at the lowest price on the site
bank.explanation: Start where demand meets proven ability. A focused design offer with real samples is easier to trust and sell.

bank.question: Which statement best shows the difference between a skill and a sellable service?
options: A skill always earns more money than a service
A service is anything you enjoy doing at home
A skill only counts if you have a certificate
A service packages a skill to solve a named client's problem
